brief.outcome: Raise trial-to-paid conversion from about 4% to 7% by the end of next quarter, counted the same way before and after, without sign-up volume falling by more than 10%.

ambition.goal_beyond: More of the freelancers who try the app become paying customers who stay, so growth does not depend on buying more sign-ups.
rungs: Improve the trial emails and the upgrade screen that exist today.
Find, from raw sign-up, product and billing records, where trial users stop and what the activation moment is, then fix onboarding, emails, the paywall and the trial length in tested steps.
Do rung 2, then keep it true with a weekly cohort check by sign-up week that flags a drop in activation or conversion, and a standing holdout so the gain is never assumed.
ambition.judge: Paid subscriptions per sign-up cohort from Stripe, for treated users against a randomised holdout, rather than the admin dashboard.

brief.deliverable: A conversion rate rebuilt from raw records, a diagnosis, changed onboarding, trial emails and paywall (and trial length if chosen) launched as randomised tests with your approval, a weekly cohort check, and an honest readout against 7%.

Funnel from sign-up to first value to paid, with hypotheses marked supported, refuted or unknown
Your chosen changes recorded with reasons
Changes built, checked and launched as randomised tests, registered before launch
Results read from Stripe against the holdout, with the sign-up volume guardrail
Weekly cohort check set up and learnings saved

answers.question: What is the product?
answers.answer: A self-serve invoicing app for freelancers.

answers.question: How many sign-ups and what trial?
answers.answer: About 2,400 trial sign-ups a month, a 14-day trial, no card required.

answers.question: What is conversion now?
answers.answer: Trial-to-paid is about 4% (admin dashboard; not checked how it is counted).

answers.question: Which tools can your AI reach?
What is the target and the limit?

research.approach: Practitioners start by rebuilding the conversion number from raw records, because dashboards differ on who is in the base and how long a payment still counts as a trial conversion. They then follow each sign-up cohort through the funnel (sign-up, first value, upgrade screen, payment) and find the activation behaviour and the days when users convert, because trial length should follow the time to value, not the other way round. Fixes are made around that moment: onboarding that gets users to it faster, emails that react to what the user did or did not do, and a paywall that appears when value is felt. Because conversion is a low-rate outcome, they size tests before starting, test bigger changes first, randomise at the user level with a holdout, and judge on payments from the billing system.

sources.title: Free trial length for SaaS (Userpilot, citing ChartMogul's January 2026 study)
sources.note: Trial length should follow time to value: find the median time from sign-up to activation and conversion by trial day. Cites ChartMogul's study of 200 products: median free-to-paid 8%, 14 days the most common length, and opt-in trials in the 4 to 6% range. Vendor blog; field results on length are marginal.

sources.title: Configure trial offers on subscriptions (Stripe Docs)
sources.note: A free trial with no card is a subscription in trialing status; what happens at trial end without a payment method (create an invoice, cancel or pause) is a setting; a trial_will_end event fires about 3 days before the end by default. Useful for counting conversions from billing records. No date on the page; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Experiment metrics (PostHog Docs)
sources.note: Seen in search results, not opened in full. Experiments run on feature flags that randomise users and record exposure; conversion windows are anchored to each user's first exposure and can run past the end date. Search summary says the page may be old. No date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Automation goals and conversion criteria (Customer.io Docs)
sources.note: Seen in search results, not opened in full. A goal can be an event or a segment change, with a conversion window of up to 90 days after delivery; exit conditions are set separately; holdout and A/B tests exist in the workflow builder. No date; accessed 2026-11-03.

steps.name: Rebuild trial-to-paid by sign-up cohort from raw records
steps.why: The 4% is unverified; payments must be counted for each sign-up month with a stated window, including late payments after the trial ends.

steps.name: Check who is really in the base: bots, duplicates, people who never opened the app
steps.why: A base full of non-users hides the true rate of the people who did try the product.

steps.name: Follow each cohort through sign-up, first value, upgrade screen and payment
steps.why: It shows the biggest leak and whether it differs by source.

steps.name: Find the activation behaviour and how long users take to reach it
steps.why: Trial length and email timing should follow the time to value.

steps.name: Ask non-converters why they did not pay
steps.why: Behaviour shows where users stop, not why; a short question to leavers can.

steps.name: Fix onboarding, trial emails and the paywall around the activation moment
steps.why: These are the levers the owner allows; each should react to what the user has done.

steps.name: Set the trial length from the activation and payment timing
steps.why: Field evidence on length is marginal, so own data decides.

steps.name: Test big changes first as randomised experiments with a holdout, sized before launch
steps.why: At about 4% a small lift needs thousands of users per arm; the sign-up guardrail needs watching too.

steps.name: Check each sign-up week's activation and conversion weekly
steps.why: It keeps a gain real after the tests end.

steps.name: Ask for a card at sign-up
steps.why: Card-required trials convert at a much higher rate in published benchmarks.

pitfalls.text: Trusting a dashboard conversion rate without knowing the base, the window and whether late payments count.
Setting trial length from convention instead of the time users take to reach value.
Running small tests on a 4% outcome and calling a winner without enough users in each group.
Trial emails that keep going after the user has acted, or that ignore what they did.
Counting an experiment's conversions only until it ends, missing payments that arrive after the trial.

stages.name: Pin down the problem
stages.goal: Turn the owner's words into a measured problem, a target, limits and the data we can reach. Writes BRIEF.md.

stages.name: Rebuild trial-to-paid from raw records
stages.goal: Join sign-ups to Stripe payments by sign-up month and rebuild the conversion rate with a written counting rule: base, window after sign-up, and treatment of late and repeat sign-ups.

checks.name: The rebuilt rate is shown next to the dashboard's 4%, and any gap of more than 0.5 points is explained by the counting rule
Payments within 14 days of sign-up and payments later than 14 days are shown separately
Rates are shown by sign-up month, and months too recent to have finished the window are marked immature

stages.name: Gather trial behaviour and email activity
stages.goal: Pull product events for each sign-up's first 21 days and the trial emails with their results, so activation timing, upgrade screen views and email effect can be read.

checks.name: Events cover the same sign-ups and dates as the conversion table
All pulls were read-only and no email was sent or activated
Any event that is not tracked, such as the upgrade screen view, is named in the notes

stages.name: Check the base and the join can be trusted
stages.goal: Find bots, duplicates and sign-ups that never opened the product, and check PostHog users match Stripe customers, before anyone reasons from the rates.

checks.name: At least 95% of paying customers in Stripe match a PostHog user by id or email, and the unmatched are listed
The share of sign-ups with no product event at all is stated, and the rate is shown both with and without them
Monthly sign-up counts from PostHog agree with the owner's 2,400 within 5%
Ends with CHECKED, LIMITED or UNRELIABLE and what that means for the diagnosis

stages.name: Find where trial users stop
stages.goal: Follow each cohort through sign-up, activation, upgrade screen and payment; find the activation behaviour and timing, the biggest leak, and differences by source. Test the hypotheses and keep competing explanations.

checks.name: Every hypothesis is SUPPORTED, REFUTED or UNKNOWN with the numbers behind it
Activation is called a correlation until a test shows that pushing users to it raises payments
Source or segment findings with fewer than 300 sign-ups are marked low-confidence
Days from sign-up to activation and to payment are shown as a distribution, with the median and the share after day 14

stages.name: Rank what to change and test
stages.goal: Turn findings into ranked change cards for onboarding, trial emails, the paywall and trial length, each with the expected effect, effort, risk, the sign-up impact and the users needed to detect it; include a short non-converter question if the data cannot explain the leak.

checks.name: Every card cites the finding it rests on
Every card states the users per group needed to detect its expected lift at 80% power, and how many weeks that takes at about 1,200 sign-ups per group per month
Every card says whether it can change sign-up volume and how that would be watched against the 10% limit
No card falls outside onboarding, emails, the paywall and trial length

stages.name: Owner chooses
stages.goal: The owner picks card ids and the order of tests. Ask for the reason when the top card is passed over, and record it.

checks.name: Chosen and passed-over cards are in decisions.jsonl
A reason is recorded wherever the top card was passed over

stages.name: Build the onboarding, email and paywall changes
stages.goal: Write the chosen onboarding steps, trial emails as Customer.io drafts keyed to what the user did or did not do, paywall copy and layout, and the trial-length variant, with exact steps for whoever ships them.

outputs.name: Email drafts with trigger, timing and exit rule

checks.name: Every change traces to a chosen card
Every email names the user action or missing action that triggers it and the action that stops it
Every email exists in Customer.io as an inactive draft and none was activated
Nothing on the paywall or in emails states a price, feature or limit that the product does not have

stages.name: Design the randomised tests
stages.goal: Fix who is randomised (new sign-ups, by user), the groups and holdout, the order of tests, the primary measure and window, the sign-up guardrail, and the stop rule.

checks.name: Assignment is random by user, recorded at first exposure, and the groups match on source within 5 points
The primary measure is a Stripe payment within a stated window after sign-up, counted the same way in every group, including payments after trial end
The size per group is calculated for the expected lift, and tests that cannot finish before the end of next quarter are merged or dropped
Weekly sign-ups are compared with the previous 8 weeks and a fall of more than 10% triggers the stop rule

stages.name: Ship the tests to new sign-ups
stages.goal: Register each test, then the owner ships the approved product changes and activates the approved emails for the test groups only, and we read back what went live.

checks.name: Each test is in experiments.jsonl with its measure, window, size and stop rule before it goes live
After the first 200 sign-ups per group, the split is within 5% of the planned ratio, and holdout users receive none of the new emails
Each shipped change and activated email was read back and matches the approved version

stages.name: Read results against Stripe and watch each cohort
stages.goal: Read each test on Stripe payments against its holdout, track sign-up volume, and keep a weekly check of activation and conversion by sign-up week that flags drops. Read-only.

checks.name: Payment counts come from Stripe records, not the admin dashboard, with the same counting rule as the baseline
A verdict is given only when each group has reached its planned size and the window has finished, otherwise INCONCLUSIVE with the confidence range
Sign-up volume and 60-day retention of converters are checked and any breach is flagged
Conversion is reported against 7% for finished cohorts only, and a miss is reported as a miss

stages.name: Keep what we learned
stages.goal: Close each experiment, save rules with their scope, and plan the next round of tests.

checks.name: Every launched test is closed in experiments.jsonl with its verdict
Each proposed rule says whether it holds for this job, this business or the playbook

hypotheses.statement: The 4% is measured differently from what the owner assumes, so the real rate is not 4%.
hypotheses.test: Rebuild the rate by sign-up month from sign-ups and Stripe payments with a stated window and compare with the dashboard.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The rebuilt rate differs from 4% by 1 point or more under the plain counting rule.
hypotheses.refute_if: The rebuilt rate is within 0.5 points of 4%.

hypotheses.statement: A large part of the 2,400 sign-ups never used the product, which drags the rate down.
hypotheses.test: Share of sign-ups with no product event in their first 7 days, and the conversion rate among those who did.
hypotheses.confirm_if: At least 30% of sign-ups have no product event.
hypotheses.refute_if: Fewer than 10% have no product event.

hypotheses.statement: Most trial users never reach the action that shows value.
hypotheses.test: Candidate activation actions from PostHog: the share of sign-ups doing each within 3 days, and payment rate for those who did against those who did not.
hypotheses.confirm_if: At least 60% of active users do not do the action in 3 days, and those who do pay at least 3 times as often.
hypotheses.refute_if: Most active users do the action, or payment rates differ by less than 1.5 times.

hypotheses.statement: The 14-day trial does not match how long users take to reach value or to decide.
hypotheses.test: Distribution of days from sign-up to activation and to payment, and payments after day 14.
hypotheses.confirm_if: At least a quarter of activated users first activate after day 7, or at least 20% of payments arrive after day 14.
hypotheses.refute_if: Most users activate within 4 days and few payments arrive after day 14.

hypotheses.statement: The trial emails run on a timer and ignore what the user has done.
hypotheses.test: List each trial email with its trigger and compare who gets it with activation status.
hypotheses.confirm_if: No email depends on activation, or activated and stalled users get the same emails.
hypotheses.refute_if: Emails already branch on activation and stalled users receive different ones.

hypotheses.statement: Users who found value never see a clear upgrade prompt before the trial ends.
hypotheses.test: Share of activated users who viewed the upgrade screen before day 14, and the share of viewers who start checkout.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Fewer than half of activated users saw the upgrade screen, or fewer than 10% of viewers start checkout.
hypotheses.refute_if: Most activated users saw it and at least 20% of viewers start checkout.

hypotheses.statement: Conversion differs a lot by source, so one cause is a mix of poor-fit sign-ups.
hypotheses.test: Conversion by sign-up source for sources with at least 300 sign-ups.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The best source converts at least twice as well as the worst, with 300 or more sign-ups each.
hypotheses.refute_if: Rates are within 30% of each other.

dropped.reason: Asking for a card at sign-up is not among the changes the owner listed and would put the sign-up volume guardrail (no more than 10% lower) at risk.

measurement.window: Each test is read once its last sign-up has had 14 days plus a stated grace window for late payments; the 7% target is read on cohorts that have finished that window, by the end of next quarter.
measurement.min_volume: Derived from the reported 4% (80% power, 5% significance): about 6,700 per group to detect 4% to 5%, 1,900 for 4% to 6%, 900 for 4% to 7%. At about 1,200 per group a month that is 6 months, 1.5 months, 3 weeks, so bigger changes go first.
measurement.stop_rule: Stop a test early if weekly sign-ups fall more than 10% below the previous 8 weeks, a message goes to the wrong group, or paid-customer retention at 60 days drops; otherwise run to the planned size.
